passage: Although the marine biologist had spent seventeen years cataloging reef formations along the Andaman ______ she acknowledged that much of the underwater terrain remained unmapped.
explanation: The sentence begins with the subordinating conjunction "Although," creating a dependent clause that must be joined to the independent clause with a comma. The option using a comma after "coast" correctly punctuates this boundary. The option using a semicolon is wrong because a semicolon cannot join a dependent clause to an independent clause. The option using a period is wrong because it turns "Although the marine biologist had spent seventeen years cataloging reef formations along the Andaman coast" into a sentence fragment. The option with no punctuation is wrong because Standard English requires a comma after an introductory dependent clause.

passage: The geochemist who identified high concentrations of lithium in the brine ______ presented her findings at a symposium in Reykjavík last October.
explanation: The subject of this sentence is "The geochemist who identified high concentrations of lithium in the brine pools," with "who identified...pools" serving as a restrictive relative clause that is essential to identifying which geochemist is meant. No punctuation should separate this restrictive clause from the main verb "presented." The option with no punctuation after "pools" is correct. The option inserting a comma incorrectly separates the subject from its verb. The option using a semicolon fractures the sentence into a fragment before the semicolon and a fragment after it. The option using a dash similarly creates an ungrammatical break between the subject and its predicate.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The architect Maren ______ who redesigned the waterfront promenade in the port city of Stavanger, was honored with Norway's highest award for urban design.
explanation: The clause "who redesigned the waterfront promenade in the port city of Stavanger" is nonrestrictive—it provides additional information about Maren Solvig, who has already been identified by name. Nonrestrictive clauses must be set off by paired punctuation. Because the closing boundary after "Stavanger" already uses a comma, the opening boundary must also use a comma: "Solvig, who redesigned...Stavanger, was honored." The option placing a comma after "Solvig" correctly opens this pair. The option with no punctuation fails to mark the nonrestrictive clause. The option using a semicolon creates a sentence fragment before the semicolon. The option using a dash creates a mismatched pair—an opening dash paired with a closing comma—which violates the convention that parenthetical punctuation must match.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: Although preliminary surveys of the cave system near Trebinje suggested that the limestone formations were relatively ______ radiocarbon dating of embedded organic material later confirmed that the oldest stalagmites had been growing for over forty thousand years.
explanation: The entire clause beginning with "Although" and ending with "recent" is a dependent clause introduced by the subordinating conjunction "Although." This dependent clause must be joined to the following independent clause with a comma. The option using a comma after "recent" is correct. The option using a semicolon is wrong because a semicolon cannot join a dependent clause to an independent clause—it requires two independent clauses. The option using a period is wrong because it turns everything from "Although" through "recent" into a sentence fragment. The option with no punctuation is wrong because a comma is required after an introductory dependent clause, especially one this long. The difficulty here lies in tracking the subordinating conjunction "Although" through the extended dependent clause with multiple embedded clauses.

passage: The collection of nineteenth-century nautical instruments ______ on permanent display at the maritime museum in Gdańsk.
explanation: The subject of this sentence is "collection," a singular noun. The prepositional phrase "of nineteenth-century nautical instruments" modifies "collection" but does not change the number of the subject. The singular present-tense verb "is" correctly agrees with "collection." The option "are" is wrong because it treats the plural "instruments" as the subject. The option "were" is wrong because it is both plural and past tense, neither of which matches the singular present-tense context. The option "have been" is wrong because it is a plural verb form that fails to agree with the singular subject "collection."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The grant proposal outlined three objectives: cataloging the butterfly species of the Dinaric Alps, ______ the migratory corridors used by alpine swifts, and publishing the results in a peer-reviewed journal.
explanation: The sentence lists three objectives in a series separated by commas: "cataloging...Alps," "______ the migratory corridors...," and "publishing...journal." Parallel structure requires that all three items in this series take the same grammatical form. Since "cataloging" and "publishing" are gerunds (present participles functioning as nouns), the second item must also be a gerund. "Mapping" maintains the parallel gerund form. "To map" breaks parallelism by switching to an infinitive. "She mapped" breaks parallelism by introducing a finite clause with a new subject. "Maps" breaks parallelism by using a simple present-tense verb rather than a gerund.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: Neither the lead conservator nor the two assistants who spent months restoring the seventeenth-century altarpiece ______ able to determine the precise origin of the pigment used in the central panel.
explanation: When "neither...nor" connects two subjects, the verb agrees in number with the subject closer to the verb. Here, "the two assistants who spent months restoring the seventeenth-century altarpiece" is the nearer subject and is plural, so the verb must be plural. "Were" is the correct plural past-tense form. "Was" is wrong because it is singular, agreeing with "conservator" rather than the nearer subject "assistants." "Has been" is wrong because it is singular. "Is" is wrong because it is both singular and present tense. The long intervening relative clause "who spent months restoring the seventeenth-century altarpiece" makes this agreement harder to track, but the rule is determined by the nearer subject in the "neither...nor" construction.

passage: Constructed entirely from reclaimed timber and hand-forged iron, ______

options.text: hikers from across the region have been attracted to the footbridge spanning the gorge near Konjic.
the gorge near Konjic is now spanned by a footbridge that has attracted hikers from across the region.

the footbridge spanning the gorge near Konjic has attracted hikers from across the region.

explanation: The introductory participial phrase "Constructed entirely from reclaimed timber and hand-forged iron" must modify the noun that immediately follows the comma—this noun must be the thing that was constructed. Only the option beginning with "the footbridge" places the correct noun in the subject position, because the footbridge is what was constructed from reclaimed timber and iron. The option beginning with "hikers" creates a dangling modifier, implying hikers were constructed from timber and iron. The option beginning with "the gorge" similarly dangles the modifier, implying the gorge was constructed. The option beginning with "attracting" places a gerund phrase as the subject, wrongly implying that the act of attracting was constructed from timber and iron.
